ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: This study investigates the morphological changes in Char Munshi, located along the lower Meghna River, Bangladesh, over the past 34 years (1989–2023) and their impact on the livelihoods of the local population. Analysis of Landsat satellite imagery, combined with social surveys, reveals that despite ongoing land erosion, significant land accretion has occurred during this period. A notable event in 1999 saw the highest erosion rate, resulting in a 25.14 km2 land loss. Over the study period, the island's area expanded approximately 42-fold, from an initial 2.44 km2 in 1989 to its current size. The accretion of land positively impacted livelihood by increasing the farmland. On the other hand, frequent riverbank erosion displaced the people, damaged their property, and reduced their long-term economic stability and social security. The findings reveal that the livelihoods of people living in the Charland are primarily dependent on agriculture and fishing. However, challenges such as erosion and cyclones disrupt their way of life, pushing many into secondary or alternative jobs. These hardships also contribute to increased school dropouts, early marriages among girls, and a rise in crime and violence, which are closely linked to economic constraints and the lack of sufficient job opportunities. This study underscores the critical need for targeted economic support, crop and land insurance, and robust erosion control measures, which are essential for bolstering the resilience of Char Munshi's vulnerable population and promoting the sustainable development of its communities.

ce:section.ce:para: Coastal morphology is an ongoing natural process in dynamic coastal zones; thus, morphological changes occur through space and time (Uddin et al., 2020). The modifications of the shape and geometry of islands due to sediment deposition and land erosion are the evolving aspects of how coastal landforms and features alter in response to natural processes (Biswas et al., 2022). Along the shorelines, the deposition of sediment is the consequence of rainfall in the upper stream especially during the monsoon season causing erosion in the upper stream, particularly in hilly areas with rough terrain, and transports a large amount of sediment downriver to plains and distributary outlets (Uddin et al., 2020; Mishra et al., 2019; Klatzel and Murray, 2009). The constant transformations in the coastal morphology owing to erosion and accretion gradually initiate the formation of deltas, which gradually transform into elevated landforms of different sizes and shapes (Uddin et al., 2020; Abdullah Al et al., 2018; Datta and Deb, 2012).

Similar to coastal regions worldwide, the coast of Bangladesh has also experienced significant morphological changes (Hoque et al., 2023; Crawford et al., 2021; Islam et al., 2020, 2010; Mullick et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2015). The deltaic plain of Bangladesh developed by the convergence of the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna (GBM) (Islam et al., 2010). It is the largest sedimentary basin ranging from river delta to shallow sea in the world (Hossain et al., 2018). The GBM rivers carry sediment of approximately 2.4 billion tons into the Bay of Bengal every year (Hoque et al., 2023). The transported sediment deposits in the floodplains resulted in morphological alterations in the coastal region (Akter et al., 2016); subsequently forming the Bengal Fan, which is considered the world’s biggest submarine fan (Hossain et al., 2018). The GBM delta, which captures the majority of Himalayas sediments, is influenced by the uplift of the Shillong Plateau in the north, tectonic activities from the Himalayan front, and the accretionary fold belt in the east (Hossain et al., 2018; Reitz et al., 2014). Additionally, the morphological changes caused by the bottom landscape of the Bay of Bengal often affect the nearby coastal region, particularly Bangladesh's shore, as the deeper Bay of Bengal receives a great quantity of sediments through undercurrents (Hoque et al., 2013, 2023; Akter et al., 2016; Mikhailov and Dotsenko, 2007; Khandker, 1997; Viles and Spencer, 1995). The coastal area near the Meghna River estuary exhibits significant morphological alterations and land formation, making it one of the most dynamic areas (Paul and Rashid, 2017). The formation of new islands has been reported at the Ganges and the Brahmaputra confluence near the estuary of the Meghna River (Uddin et al., 2020; Abdullah et al., 2019; Brammer, 2014; Jakobsen et al., 2002). The Charlands (matured sandbars) connect to the riverbank or form islands in the middle of the river (Rahman and Rahman, 2011).

Bhola is situated at the Meghna River estuary (Toa and Ali, 2022), which is considered a morphologically dynamic island due to the accretion and erosional cycle triggered by GBM river systems (Anwar and Rahman, 2021). From 1973 to 2010, the Bhola island experienced an annual gain of an average of 15 km2 each year as the eastern side faced erosion and the accretion occurred on the west and upper north sides (Galib and Moniruzzaman, 2017; Krantz, 1999). Erosion in the coastal zone has been recognized as a significant ecological concern around the world in the coastal zone (Ashraful Islam et al., 2016). Tropical cyclones, forest degradation, and the shifting position of distributary outlets are the most prevalent causes of erosion, while landfill initiatives and an abundance of sediment deposits cause accretion near the estuary (Hossain et al., 2023; Ve et al., 2021). An additional almost 769.4 km2 of land has been encompassed into this region and its surroundings from 1977 to 2010 (Islam et al., 2015). Bangladesh’s total area expands by approximately 20 km2 annually, potentially accumulating over 1000 km2 in the next 50 years (Chaturvedi and Sakhuja, 2015). While the Meghna estuary's huge silt subsidizes the deposit, the land is also being eroded by the tremendous tidal surges occurring there (Toa and Ali, 2022; Sarwar and Woodroffe, 2013). It is claimed that Bhola Island has changed in area and shape since 1960 due to sea levels rising and land erosion (Toa and Ali, 2022). Moreover, the sea level rise poses a significant threat to Bangladesh’s coastal areas, as it has a flat topography characterized by wide and narrow ridges and valleys (Shariot-Ullah, 2024).

The 109 rivers and coastal Charlands, home to about 10 million people, cover around 10 % of Bangladesh's total area (Siddique, 2022; Imran Khan, 2018). Newly formed Charlands offer new opportunities for the livelihood of poverty-stricken people, and they became homes to many people who have been displaced from their prior lands due to river bank erosion (Demaine, 2021). Coastal chars usually take about 10 years to become resilient enough for permanent human habitation once they form, and they frequently modify throughout time (Carvajal et al., 2011). In the earliest phases of stability, intensive livestock husbandry and different kinds of fisheries are the major sources of subsistence (Demaine, 2021). The riverbank erosion consequences are severe, including the loss of land, displacement of communities, social exclusion, and adverse impacts on both physical and psychological health (Kaiser, 2023). Moreover, these disasters result in the displacement of several inhabitants who reside in those Charlands, leading to the loss of their assets and means of sustenance, hence increasing their susceptibility (Mahmood et al., 2020). Moreover, an analysis of gauge data from 1985 to 2000 shows that the rising mean sea level is at an annual rate of 3.15 mm due to climate change, significantly higher than the current global average of 2 mm per year (Sarwar, 2005). This rate of increase is much worse than the projected increase of 1.5 m in sea level across the coastline of Bangladesh by 2030 would have a significant impact on around 22,000 km2 of land and influence the lives of almost 17 million people, accounting for 15 % of the total population (Toa and Ali, 2022; Hazra et al., 2002).

The study of morphological behaviors plays a crucial role in the sustainable management of coastal zones and, more importantly, its effect on the livelihood of char inhabitants (Hoque et al., 2023). In this regard, one of the important criteria for sustainable land use is the precise erosion and accretion data for the evaluation of alterations in the past and future trends (Natarajan et al., 2021). Traditional survey techniques are laborious, time-consuming, and expensive (Ghosh et al., 2015). Whereas remotely sensed data is easily accessible, comes in both high temporal and spatial resolution, and is relatively simple to process (Islam et al., 2021). Thus, many researchers have utilized remote sensing data to monitor and analyze the morphological behaviors of riverine islands or Charlands both at home and abroad (Hoque et al., 2023; Toa and Ali, 2022; Mullick et al., 2020; Abdullah et al., 2019; Salauddin et al., 2018; Emran et al., 2017; Galib and Moniruzzaman, 2017; Paul and Rashid, 2017; Ashraful Islam et al., 2016; Md. A. Islam et al., 2015). The magnitude and nature of alterations occurring in riverine islands may be seen through temporal analysis of satellite photos (Hoque et al., 2023).

The correlation of a drainage basin's elevation and its horizontal cross-section area is referred to as hypsometry analysis and it can be represented graphically as a “hypsometric curve (HC)”, or quantitatively as “hypsometric integral (HI)” (Farhan et al., 2016). HC of a watershed basin indicates the distribution of areas with elevations (Luo, 1998). Thus, the temporal alterations in the slope of the watershed can be interpreted through the shape of the HC (Singh et al., 2008).

The area under the HC is used to compute the HI (Farhan et al., 2016). Strahler (1952b) analyzed the shapes of HC of numerous drainage basins and classified them according to their geomorphic evolution stage: the youth stage with convex upward curves (HI ≥ 0.60); the mature stage with S-shaped curves, concave upward at higher elevations and convex downward at lower elevations (0.30 ≤ HI ≤ 0.60); and the monadnock stage with concave upward curves (HI ≤ 0.30) (Farhan et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2008). The HC and HI serve as important metrics for assessing the stages of geomorphic evolution (Farhan et al., 2016).

This study addresses the unique dynamics of Char Munshi, a newly emergent charland in the lower Meghna estuary, unlike previous studies that focus on coastal erosion and accretion affecting human settlements, this study specifically examines the morphological developments of Char Munshi and their impact on the local population's livelihoods over time. This comprehensive examination fills a critical research gap, underscoring the necessity of understanding these dynamics for sustainable development and policy-making.

The primary objective of this study is to investigate the morphological changes in Char Munshi over the past 34 years (1989–2023) using satellite imagery. Additionally, it aims to examine how these changes have affected the socio-economic status of the local population.

Char Munshi is situated at the lower Meghna River beside the north-eastern part of Bhola island and its geographical location is 22.730350°N latitude and 90.6714672°E longitude (Fig. 1). It is located in Daulat Khan Upazila, Bhola, and is part of the Madanpur Union (BBS, 2013). This char was first discovered on a satellite image in 1989; thus, it is considered to be in the mature mangrove forests or settlements of development (Sarker et al., 2021).

Char Munshi's climate is classified as a tropical monsoon climate (Am) under the updated Köppen-Geiger climate classification (Beck et al., 2023). Bhola, and by extension experiences significant fluctuations in monthly rainfall due to its severe seasonal variance (Weather Spark, 2024). The island receives approximately 2297.4 mm of rainfall annually, averaging 191.4 mm per month over around 123 rainy days each year (Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD)). The duration of the rainy season spans almost 10 months, commencing in mid-February and concluding in early December (Weather Spark, 2024). According to BMD, June is the wettest month in Bhola, with an average precipitation of 465.2 mm. The rainless season extends from early December to mid-February, affecting agricultural practices and water resources (Weather Spark, 2024). January, in particular, is the driest month, with an average rainfall of 10.3 mm (BMD).

Given its proximity to the Meghna River estuary, Char Munshi is regarded as unstable since this region is very morphologically dynamic (Paul and Rashid, 2017). Few works have been done along the shoreline and other more mature islands on the coast of Bangladesh (Hoque et al., 2023; Toa and Ali, 2022; Uddin et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2015). However, no previous work has been done here about how morphological behavior affects the livelihood pattern of the inhabitants of Char Munshi.

This study conducted an in-depth household survey among the native inhabitants of Char Munshi in the Bhola district. Primary data were meticulously collected through a combination of direct observation, focus group discussions (FGDs), and a structured questionnaire. The survey encompassed various critical aspects, including livelihood patterns, health issues, transportation systems, and water sources.

In this study, respondents were chosen through simple random sampling. This approach is particularly effective as it ensures that each individual among the residents has an equal opportunity to be selected (Singh, 2003). As a result, this method minimizes selection bias and improves the overall representativeness of the sample (Noor et al., 2022).

To determine the appropriate sample size, Yamane's (1967):886) sampling method was employed. The formula provided by Yamane is as follows (Eq. 1), assuming a 95 % confidence level and a 5 % margin of error (e=0.05).(1)n=N1+N(e2)Where n = sample size, N = population size, and e = level of precision.
Using this formula, the calculated sample size for the study was approximately 377 respondents.
The collected data were analyzed statistically using the SPSS.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Collection, processing, and analysis of satellite images
ce:section.ce:para: Satellite imagery is a valuable tool for capturing detailed observations of the Earth's surface (Khorram et al., 2017). This study utilized satellite images from Landsat 5, Landsat 8, and Landsat 9 to monitor and analyze the morphological changes in Char Munshi (Table 1).

A systematic framework was followed for the processing and analysis of satellite data (Fig. 2). Initially, raw satellite data sourced from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) underwent essential pre-processing steps, which included radiometric calibration and atmospheric correction for each composite image band, utilizing ArcGIS 10.8. Following this, the study area was carefully extracted from the composite images. This step involved isolating Char Munshi, the region of interest, from the broader satellite imagery to focus specifically on local changes.

Subsequently, unsupervised classification techniques were employed on the extracted images to identify various land cover types and detect changes over time. This classification process facilitated the differentiation between land and water and helped to identify patterns of land accretion and erosion. Finally, temporal change detection analysis was conducted to quantify the morphological changes in Char Munshi from 1989 to 2023. This analysis involved comparing satellite images from different years to track the progression of land accretion and erosion over time.

By integrating these methods, the study provided a detailed and accurate representation of the morphological changes occurring in Char Munshi, contributing to a better understanding of its dynamic landscape.

Langbein (1947) pioneered the use of hypsometric analysis to illustrate the general slope and shape of drainage basins (Kadlag et al., 2022). Hypsometric analysis for Char Munshi was conducted using GIS and RS techniques with ALOS PALSAR DEM data at a 30 m spectral resolution in the QGIS 3.34 environment. The HC was plotted by attribute feature classes that contained the elevation profile and the area. The HI was computed by incorporating the elevation-relief ratio technique proposed by Pike and Wilson (1971), following Eq. (2) (Shekar and Mathew, 2022; Farhan et al., 2016).(2)E≈HI=Elevmean−ElevminElevmax−Elevmin
HI controls the HC shape and indicates the volume of an uneroded watershed since it is the area under the HC (Valkanou et al., 2020).

Char Munshi has experienced both erosion and accretion over the years, with significant changes in land area (Fig. 3). In 1989, Char Munshi emerged in the lower of the Meghna River near Bhola District. Initially covering only 2.44 km2 and was uninhabitable (Table 2). From 1989 to 1994, the island experienced minimal erosion but significant accretion (47.06 km2). As a result, the land area expanded due to sediment deposition. In 1999, Char Munshi covered a total area of 42.65 km2, which decreased by 14 % from 1994 due to more erosion than accretion. The north and south sides of Char Munshi have experienced erosion, resulting in a net loss of land area. Conversely, the east side has experienced accretion (Fig. 3b). In 2004, the total area of Char Munshi increased due to more accretion than erosion from 1999 to 2004. During this period, the north and east sides see erosion but the north-western and south sides see more accretion.

In 2009, the total area of Char Munshi was 54.73 km2 which was less than the total area in 2004. From 2004 to 2009, all sides experienced erosion especially the south portion while the north portion gained some area. Between 2009 and 2014, the area experienced a net accretion of 36.05 km2, with the northern and eastern sides showing more significant growth. However, there was also erosion of 13.7 km2 on the northern and southern sides. In 2019, the total area of Char Munshi experienced a 10 % reduction compared to 2014. There was 15.9 km2 of accreted land as the east side experienced more growth of the area, while 23.67 km2 eroded from the north and west sides especially. The unchanged area in 2019 was 53.41 km2, representing 69 % of the total area and showing a 130 % increase compared to the unchanged area in 2014. From 2019 to 2023, the Char Munshi experienced more accretion than erosion resulting in a net increase of approximately 45.07 km2 in land area. Notably, the eastern and southern sides experienced substantial accretion, contributing to the overall expansion of the area.

The area-elevation curve illustrates the distribution of elevation and area within the given area (Fig. 4a). The elevation value of char Munshi ranges from 0 m to 9.17 m. Notably, there is a significant inflection point at 3 m elevation since this category contains the biggest amount of landmass of the total area.

The HC for char Munshi demonstrates an S-shaped curve indicating a mature stage of geomorphic development (Fig. 4b). The curve steepens swiftly at lower elevations, exhibiting a preponderance of erosional processes in these regions. In contrast, the curve flattens at higher elevations, revealing a prevalence of depositional processes.

Char Munshi has an HI value of 0.45, signifying a mature stage of geomorphic development. This value indicates that 45 % of the original rock masses are still present in the region. The region exhibits an equilibrium between erosion and natural uplift. The landscape is being worn away by erosion while being gradually raised by tectonic forces. The region's landscapes are kept in a dynamic balance by the interaction of eroding forces and rising land.

According to survey results, the majority of residents (77.1 %) earn between 5000 and 10000 BDT (Bangladeshi Taka) (approximately $1 = 118 BDT) monthly. An additional 20 % fall into the 10000–15000 BDT income range, while only 2.9 % earn more than 20000 BDT per month. Agriculture significantly contributes to the local economy, engaging nearly 55 % of the population due to fertile land replenished by alluvial deposits during the rainy season. Fishing is the second most common occupation, involving approximately 23 % of the population. Business-related occupations are less prevalent, accounting for only 2.9 % of residents, likely due to economic constraints. The remaining 20 % are engaged in various other professions, including sailing, day labor, cobbling, and tailoring.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect on the economic condition of the char dwellers
ce:section.ce:para: A survey on Char Munshi revealed that 57 % of dwellers engage in secondary occupations due to economic constraints. Among these, 45 % work as fishermen, 25 % as farmers, 15 % as day laborers, and 5 % pursue business ventures, with the remainder lacking a fixed secondary occupation. This highlights the island’s economic challenges and the various ways residents supplement their primary incomes.

Table 3 shows a moderate positive correlation between occupation and income, indicating that higher occupation levels correspond with increased income. In Char Munshi, fishermen, and businessmen have the highest incomes, while farmers earn the least, primarily due to land erosion causing loss of cultivated land and necessitating supplementary economic activities.

Survey results show significant variation in the ability to meet basic needs based on occupation. Only 42.1 % of farmers and 12.5 % of fishermen can fulfill their family's basic needs, whereas 57.9 % of farmers and 87.5 % of fishermen cannot. When primary occupations fail to provide sufficient income, dwellers turn to secondary occupations to sustain their families.
Table 4 indicates a negative correlation between occupation and the ability to meet basic needs. As occupation changes, the ability to fulfill basic needs changes inversely.

Table 5 presents a moderate positive correlation between reasons for occupation change and land erosion. Increased occupation change reasons correspond with heightened land erosion. Many dwellers, affected by erosion, switch occupations or take on additional activities to survive. Approximately 9.38 % have changed their occupations due to erosion, with many relying on secondary occupations for income.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Impact of morphological changes on the livelihood pattern of the char dwellers
ce:section.ce:para: In Char Munshi, river networks are the primary means of communication, with people relying on engine boats for travel to the char. The boat, the only vehicle from the Bhola mainland to Char Munshi, operates three times daily. Passengers sometimes wait over an hour for it to fill up. Erosion often necessitates route changes, causing the boatman to travel longer distances due to the emergence of new Chars, resulting in extended travel times. Within Char Munshi, there is no public transportation, and residents must walk on unpaved mud paths. Constructing paved roads is impractical and unsustainable due to unpredictable erosion.

Erosion poses significant challenges for residents, particularly farmers who rely on fishing and farming for their livelihoods. Many families struggle with poverty and have limited land for cultivation. Loss of cultivated land due to erosion forces them to seek assistance from NGOs or government organizations.

Every year, numerous families lose their homes to erosion, leaving them without shelter or belongings. Rebuilding is an immense challenge without savings or resources, leading many to seek refuge with relatives or migrate elsewhere.

Significant sedimentation during the monsoon season leads to the creation of new landforms called "chars" in the river delta. However, these newly accreted lands often fall under the control of influential people, causing conflicts among residents. Initially, these new lands serve as pastures for domestic animals and gradually become suitable for cultivating paddy and vegetables.

Land erosion has left the poor residents of Char Munshi without their cultivated land, which was their only source of living. Consequently, providing education for their children becomes a major challenge for homeless or landless families. Survey results indicate that approximately 44 % of residents had to interrupt their children's education due to these economic hardships, while 56 % managed to continue schooling.

The poor community struggles to meet basic needs due to limited income. Erosion has worsened their difficulty, leaving them with no land to live. Consequently, many parents helplessly marry off their daughters at an early age, hoping to secure their future. Among 40 female respondents, 23 reported early marriages due to their families’ poor economic conditions, while 17 attributed them to parental unawareness.

Family breakups are another consequence of erosion, as some dwellers lose their only homes and become shelterless. This situation often leads to decisions to reduce family size by separating from older family members, resulting in broken families. Approximately 3 % of respondents reported family breakups due to the destruction of their homes.

The loss of homes or cultivated land also leads to various family problems, including domestic violence and social crime. Homeless poor individuals often claim dowries from their in-laws, and those who lose their means of subsistence may resort to violence. Furthermore, erosion-induced destruction of homes disproportionately affects female family members, leaving them vulnerable to security issues. Unfortunately, finding solutions to these complex problems remains challenging for many affected residents.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the morphological changes in Char Munshi over the past 34 years. Significant changes were observed from 1989, when the island first emerged in the lower Meghna River, to 2023. These morphological changes include accretion and erosion of land and shorelines. During the study period, net accretion around the island has been substantial, largely due to sediment deposition from the Himalayas (Uddin et al., 2020), increasing the island's area. Similar deposition trends have been observed in other coastal areas (Hoque et al., 2023; Pape et al., 2010). However, the erosional process is also significant (Uddin et al., 2020; Brammer, 2014), making the island highly susceptible to coastal erosion. The processes of accretion and erosion occurred on a rotational basis, consistent with trends reported by SPARRSO (1987), (1993). Tătui and Constantin (2020) suggest that the occurrence of erosion and accretion of land may be due to the annual and seasonal dynamics of coastal morphology.

Char Munshi expanded in all directions, particularly to the north and south, by receiving sediment from the Meghna River till 1994, as it is located in the northeastern region of Bhola (Toa and Ali, 2022). After 1994, the island began to experience erosion on the northern side, with accretion occurring on the eastern and southern sides, shifting the island more toward the Bay of Bengal. Similar findings were reported by Hoque et al. (2023) on the southeastern portion of Sonadia Island. The most convincing explanations for the observed physical alterations in the island are sediment supply, tidal waves, and morphological processes (Uddin et al., 2020; Brown and Nicholls, 2015), with accretion and locational adjustments being particularly significant over the years. In addition to erosion and accretion, Ali (1979), (1995) proposed that monsoon currents, discharge currents, storm surges, and tides are the main factors causing changes in the morphology of the Char Munshi.

The HC of the study area exhibits a pronounced S-shape, indicative of a mature landscape. It represents a balance between erosion and uplift processes, leading to a rather stable environment and a well-developed drainage network. Concave upward at higher altitudes illustrates the dominance of erosional processes, since the steep slopes and high relief contribute to fast erosion and sediment transport (Markose and Jayappa, 2011). Convex downhill at lower altitudes implies a dominance of depositional processes, since gentler slopes and lower relief enable sediment to accumulate. A mature landscape is formed at the intersection of these two portions, which symbolizes a balance between erosion and uplift. This trend aligns with the results of earlier research on mature landscapes (Schumm, 1956; Strahler, 1952a). The HI influences the HC and offers insights into landform alteration of the study area. Low HI values are associated with older, eroded landscapes indicating mass removal of materials by erosion (Markose and Jayappa, 2011). Singh et al. (2008), reported that regions with mature stages of development are often located at lower altitudes which can be due to anthropogenic activities, intensive farming, and deforestation alongside the natural processes.

There is an income inequality among farmers and people in other occupations, as erosion frequently causes farmers to lose their cultivated land, forcing them to shift occupations. Based on survey analysis, they often struggle to earn enough to meet their families’ basic needs and frequently supplement their earnings by engaging in fishing. Rahman and Gain (2019) and Barua et al. (2019) reported similar findings and also mentioned the shift in occupations and decreasing income levels due to the lack of available work.

The nation's total land growth may benefit from the governance of new islands. This affects development and sustainability outcomes (Brown and Nicholls, 2015). According to Abdullah et al. (2019), the large population of Bangladesh relies on integrated freshwater and maritime systems for sustenance and access to food. Thus, for a densely populated nation with a limited land area like Bangladesh, newly emerged islands are crucial (Uddin et al., 2020). The direct relationship between land availability and economic growth, food production, and overall human development is very prominent and should be utilized for sustainable growth (Sarker et al., 2018).

The findings of our study align with existing scholarly research, which underscores the importance of effectively understanding and managing the dynamic morphological changes in Char Munshi. Such efforts are vital for promoting the sustainable development of the region and enhancing the resilience of its inhabitants' livelihoods.

The study identified shoreline and land cover changes to understand processes such as erosion and accretion. The findings revealed substantial land loss and gain over time due to these processes. The study concluded that erosion and accretion are persistent phenomena in the study area. Erosion negatively impacts the economy and disrupts social life, as it strips away valuable land, whereas accretion offers new opportunities with its fertile soil. This study elucidates several critical findings that illustrate how the dynamics of erosion and accretion affect island dwellers, highlighting the vulnerability of different professions and their resultant incomes. The results indicate that from 1989 to 2023, the patterns of erosion and accretion fluctuated due to the island's dynamic nature, with accretion ultimately prevailing during the study period. According to hypsometry analysis, the geomorphic development of Char Munshi reflects a mature stage characterized by a balance between erosional and depositional processes. The S-shaped HC curve and the HI value of 0.45 signify a stable topography with substantial preservation of original rock masses. The socioeconomic data of the respondents reveal that a significant majority (77 %) live close to below the poverty line, with most engaged in agriculture and fishing as their primary economic activities. Notably, the study finds that farmers are particularly vulnerable compared to other professions; when their cultivated land is eroded, they are often compelled to shift to different occupations. Our analysis further reveals that only 42.10 % of farmers and 12.50 % of fishermen can meet their basic needs with their current income, leading them to seek supplementary work. Additionally, many respondents have permanently changed professions due to the island's erosive nature. Alarmingly, the economic conditions have led many parents to discontinue their children's education, resulting in increased school dropout rates and early marriages for daughters. This study will help the decision-makers and government-related organizations in devising effective strategies to support the vulnerable population of Charland. These strategies may include economic incentives, crop and land insurance, and the formulation of relevant laws to control erosion. Additionally, microcredit organizations could offer loans with minimal or no interest during difficult times, thereby assisting island dwellers in maintaining their livelihoods. Local administrations could implement measures to prevent an increase in school dropouts and discourage early marriages by ensuring that poor families have the necessary support and resources.
This manuscript does not contain any studies with animals performed by any of the authors.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Declaration of Generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process
ce:section.ce:para: During the preparation of this work, the authors used ChatGPT by OpenAI and Copilot by Microsoft in order to assist with refining the language, grammar, and overall cohesiveness of the manuscript.
